analysis.one_liner: Makes in-state public college debt-free by covering every student's unmet financial need.
analysis.headline: Referred to the House Education and Workforce Committee the day it was introduced with 12 Democratic cosponsors, the bill never received a hearing, markup, or vote before the Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have created a federal-state partnership in which Washington matches state investment in public higher education so that every eligible student at an in-state public college has their full unmet financial need covered by grants instead of loans. Participating states would have to cap tuition at 2023 levels and maintain their own funding. It also would have funded debt-free aid at HBCUs, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions, and extended federal student aid eligibility to Dreamer students, authorizing $84 billion in its first year.
analysis.who_benefits: Low- and middle-income students at in-state public colleges — starting with Pell Grant recipients — would have their unmet financial need covered by grants, meaning they could attend without borrowing. Students at HBCUs, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions would get grant aid covering their unmet need, and all public college students in participating states would benefit from tuition capped at 2023 levels. Dreamer students would gain federal financial aid eligibility for the first time.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Education Department to award states grants equal to their own investment in public higher education, so federal and state money together cover each eligible student's unmet need — the gap between the cost of attendance and the student's expected contribution plus grant aid — at in-state public colleges.
Prioritizes Pell Grant recipients for the aid, lets states use leftover funds for other needy students, and forbids states from counting private loans against a student's need.

Caps tuition and fees at participating public colleges at their levels on enactment, with only inflation-based increases allowed, and requires states to maintain their funding of public higher education.

Creates a separate grant program — $3 billion in its first year — for HBCUs, tribal colleges, and minority-serving institutions, with 95 percent of the money required to go directly to covering students' unmet need.
Makes Dreamer students — those who entered the U.S. before age 16 and meet education or military-service criteria — eligible for federal student aid.
Requires 4 percent of state grant funds to pay for student success programs at public colleges: advisors, tutors, childcare, transportation, and emergency microgrants.

analysis.who_pays: Federal taxpayers, through a new program authorized at $84 billion for its first year plus $3 billion for minority-serving institutions and 'such sums as may be necessary' through 2033. State governments must keep funding public colleges at recent levels and hold tuition flat. Public universities give up the ability to raise tuition beyond inflation, and institutions that break grant terms face withheld funds or fines.

drawbacks.text: Authorizes $84 billion for fiscal 2024 and 'such sums as may be necessary' each year through 2033, on top of $3 billion for HBCU and minority-serving grants — a large, open-ended new federal commitment with no dedicated funding source.

If Congress appropriates less than the formula requires, every state's grant is ratably reduced, so full debt-free coverage could fall short even if the bill became law; states can also seek waivers extending the five-year deadline.

Public institutions must freeze tuition at 2023 levels with only inflation-based increases, which could squeeze budgets if state or federal support lags; institutions that breach grant terms face probation, withheld funds, or fines.

It extends federal student aid eligibility to Dreamer students, a population currently excluded from Title IV aid — an expansion that adds cost and that the bill's sponsor list suggests would face unified opposition from the House majority.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefit is direct and large: students who now cover the gap between college costs and their aid with loans would instead have it granted, and tuition would stop rising faster than inflation at participating schools. The cost is equally real — an open-ended authorization starting near $87 billion a year — and the design depends on states opting in and on Congress actually appropriating the money, since shortfalls trigger proportional cuts to every state. The guardrails (tuition caps, maintenance-of-effort rules, escrowed aid if a state withdraws) are genuine, but the bill's success would have hinged entirely on annual appropriations it did not guarantee.

outcome.mechanism: It went to the House Education and Workforce Committee the same day it was introduced, was never scheduled for a hearing or vote, and died when the Congress ended in January 2025.

narrative.text: Rep. Mark Pocan introduced the bill on June 7, 2023 with nine original cosponsors listed on the bill; the House referred it that day to the Committee on Education and the Workforce.
That referral was the final recorded action: the committee's history shows no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action for the rest of the Congress.
The bill finished with 12 cosponsors, all of them Democrats, and expired when the 118th Congress ended on January 3, 2025.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: No one gained a new benefit: the outcome left in place the system the bill would have replaced, in which students borrow to cover unmet need and Washington spends nothing on debt-free college. The sectors that would have lost — student loan servicers and for-profit and private nonprofit colleges competing for the same students — were spared the competition it would have created.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Status quo: students keep borrowing, nothing changes

for.name: Rep. Mark Pocan
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill with nine original cosponsors and led it through its two-year life in committee.

for.name: House Democratic cosponsors
for.role: 12 cosponsors, including the nine listed at introduction (Pressley, Williams of Georgia, Boyle, Clarke of New York, Chu, Carter of Louisiana, Watson Coleman, Jayapal, Norton)
for.what_they_did: Signed on in support; no Republican ever did, and the bill ended with 12 Democratic cosponsors.

against.name: House Committee on Education and the Workforce
against.role: Sole committee of referral in the 118th Congress
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on June 7, 2023; the recorded history shows no hearing, markup, or vote, and the bill sat until the Congress ended.

against.name: Rep. Virginia Foxx
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: As chair, controlled the committee's agenda; no hearing or markup on the bill was ever scheduled.

sides.party_line_note: Support was entirely Democratic — all 12 cosponsors were Democrats [S4] — and the Republican-chaired committee of referral never took action [S5].

industries.note: Federal grant dollars would flow into state systems and their students, with reserved set-asides for student success programs, faculty hiring, and capacity; in exchange, institutions would have to cap tuition increases at the inflation rate. The new funding dwarfs the cap constraint, so the sector comes out well ahead.

The bill replaces borrowing with grant aid exactly where students take on loans — the unmet need — so the volume of student debt the industry services would shrink. Its interest in keeping the current arrangement runs against students who would rather have grants.

No grant dollars go to them: partnership funds support public institutions only, and the minority-serving grant program is limited to nonprofit and tribal institutions, explicitly excluding schools that converted from for-profit status within 25 years. A debt-free public option would also compete directly for their students.

industries.industry: Private nonprofit colleges (outside the HBCU/MSI programs)
industries.note: The bill sends new aid only to public, HBCU, tribal, and minority-serving institutions, and a guarantee that in-state public college is debt-free gives price-conscious students a strong reason to choose it. These schools would get no offsetting benefit.
